name: Human Habits
tagline: Build routines that fit real life. Start small, make the next step easier, and keep showing up.

about.statement: The habits you practice can become evidence of the person you are choosing to be.
about.bio: Human Habits is a practical guide to building routines that support the life you want. It brings together five useful ideas: identity, cues, small actions, a supportive environment, and reflection.
about.method: There is no perfect streak or one-size-fits-all routine here. Begin with one meaningful action, make it easy to start, and use what you learn to shape the next step.

habitLoop.title: Act from identity
habitLoop.description: Choose a habit that reflects the kind of person you want to become, then let each small action reinforce that direction.
habitLoop.alt: A woman exercising on a treadmill

habitLoop.title: Use clear cues
habitLoop.description: Make the moment to act visible and specific. Link a new behavior to a place, time, or routine you already notice.
habitLoop.alt: A person practicing a mindful seated pose

habitLoop.title: Start with a small action
habitLoop.description: Lower the first step until it feels possible on an ordinary day. Repetition can grow from a manageable beginning.
habitLoop.alt: A person setting out a yoga mat and exercise equipment

habitLoop.title: Shape your environment
habitLoop.description: Reduce friction for the habits you want to practice and add distance from the behaviors you want to do less often.
habitLoop.alt: A runner checking a fitness watch

habitLoop.title: Track and reflect
habitLoop.description: Notice what you did and what made it easier or harder. Use that information to adjust your next step without judgment.
habitLoop.alt: Two people stretching in a sunlit studio

principles.title: Build identity through action
principles.description: Start with a behavior that feels connected to who you want to be. Small, repeated choices make that identity tangible.
principles.alt: A woman exercising on a treadmill

principles.title: Make cues visible
principles.description: Use an existing routine, a time, or a place as a clear reminder to begin.
principles.alt: A person beside a mat and exercise equipment

principles.title: Lower the starting effort
principles.description: Make the first action small enough to fit a normal day, not just an unusually easy one.
principles.alt: A runner checking a fitness watch

principles.title: Learn from what happens
principles.description: Reflect on the environment, barriers, and progress. Change your setup instead of blaming yourself.
principles.alt: A person stretching on a mat

faq.q: How long does it take to build a habit?
faq.a: There is no fixed number of days that works for everyone. Repetition in a stable context can make an action feel more automatic over time, but the pace varies with the person, the behavior, and the circumstances.

faq.q: What if I miss a day?
faq.a: A missed day does not erase your progress. Notice what made the routine difficult, then choose the next realistic opportunity to return. You do not need to compensate or punish yourself.

faq.q: Should I start with several habits at once?
faq.a: If you are unsure, begin with one small action. A narrow focus makes it easier to find a useful cue, reduce friction, and learn what fits your day before adding more.

faq.q: What if I do not feel motivated?
faq.a: Motivation changes. Make the action smaller, prepare your environment, or link it to something you already do. The goal is not to force yourself; it is to make starting more workable.

faq.q: Are these ideas a substitute for professional care?
faq.a: No. These are general educational ideas for everyday routines, not medical or mental-health advice. If a habit or health concern is affecting you, consider speaking with a qualified professional.
